paper.title: Altered reproductive hormone profiles in systemic lupus erythematosus - A systematic review and meta-analysis.
paper.abstract:
Background

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) shows a marked female predominance during reproductive years, possibly suggesting hormonal factors in its pathogenesis. However, evidence regarding reproductive hormone alterations in SLE remains inconsistent.

Objectives

To systematically review studies assessing reproductive hormone levels in adult SLE patients compared with healthy controls and across disease activity states.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines and a pre-registered protocol (PROSPERO CRD42024544730), PubMed and Scopus were searched (May 2024). Eligible observational studies reported estradiol, testosterone, progesterone, prolactin, FSH, LH, DHEA-S, DHEA or androstenedione in SLE patients versus controls or by disease activity. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted.

Results

Eighty-three studies were included (5389 individuals for SLE vs. controls; 2067 for active vs. inactive SLE). Prolactin was consistently higher in SLE (MD 8.07 ng/mL; 95% CI 4.69-11.45; p < 0.001) and even more during flare (MD 5.83 ng/mL; 95% CI 3.88-7.78; p < 0.001). Estradiol showed non-significant overall elevations but was significantly higher in women with active disease (MD 8.55 pg/mL; 95% CI 1.37-15.73; p = 0.03). DHEA-S was found to be significantly lower in SLE (MD -1.00 μg/mL; 95% CI -1.5 to -0.50; p = 0.002) but too few studies evaluated its dynamics during flares. FSH and LH were significantly higher in men with SLE. Other hormones were inconsistent. Only three small heterogeneous studies evaluated hormonal changes during flares.

Conclusions

Prolactin excess and androgen deficiency are consistent features of SLE, particularly in women, while elevated gonadotropins are mainly seen in men. Estradiol is higher during active disease but other data are inconsistent. Longitudinal studies are limited, with prolactin the only hormone consistently linked to disease activity and full hormonal profiles during flares are largely unstudied.

problem.title: Reproductive hormone alterations in systemic lupus erythematosus are poorly understood, especially during disease flares
problem.summary: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) disproportionately affects women of reproductive age, suggesting a hormonal role in its pathogenesis. A meta-analysis of 83 studies found prolactin excess and androgen (DHEA-S) deficiency were consistent features in SLE, while estradiol was elevated during active disease, but most other hormone findings were inconsistent across studies.
problem.affected_women: Women of reproductive age with systemic lupus erythematosus

data_need.description: Longitudinal data on full reproductive hormone profiles during SLE flares, tracked over time in the same patients
data_need.why_it_matters: Without longitudinal flare data, it is unclear whether hormonal changes drive disease activity or merely accompany it, limiting the ability to use hormones for monitoring or treatment.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states that 'Only three small heterogeneous studies evaluated hormonal changes during flares' and concludes that 'full hormonal profiles during flares are largely unstudied,' indicating a clear absence of longitudinal evidence.

verification.findings: My single search attempt failed due to a tool error (server search limit exceeded), so no results could be reviewed. I cannot confirm or deny whether new longitudinal data on full reproductive hormone profiles during SLE flares has been collected since the source publication.

paper.title: Ultra-processed food consumption and risk of infertility in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
paper.abstract:
Background

Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been linked to multiple adverse health outcomes; however, their association with infertility remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the relationship between UPF consumption and infertility risk in adults.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 31, 2026. Eligible studies assessed UPF intake using validated dietary assessment tools based on the NOVA classification and reported infertility outcomes among adults aged ≥18 years. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic.

Results

Four studies providing five independent effect estimates and including 8,769 participants (8,118 women and 651 men) were included. In the random-effects model, higher UPF consumption was not significantly associated with infertility risk (RR = 1.26, 95% CI: 0.94-1.69), although the point estimate suggested a positive direction of association. Substantial between-study heterogeneity was present (I2  = 72.0%, p = 0.006). In sex-stratified analyses, no significant association was observed among women (RR = 1.26, 95% CI: 0.79-2.00; I2  = 68.4%). Subgroup analyses by study design and exposure assessment yielded no statistically significant associations under random-effects models.

Conclusion

Current evidence does not show a statistically robust association between UPF consumption and infertility under random-effects models, although estimates consistently suggest a positive trend. Evidence remains limited by few studies, substantial heterogeneity, and self-reported outcomes. Larger prospective, sex-specific studies are needed.

problem.title: It is unclear whether eating more ultra-processed food raises the risk of infertility
problem.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of four studies examined whether ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption is linked to infertility risk in adults. Pooled results showed a positive but statistically non-significant association overall and among women, with substantial heterogeneity between studies. The authors conclude current evidence does not robustly establish this link.
problem.affected_women: Adult women assessed for infertility outcomes in dietary studies, comprising most of the study population (8,118 of 8,769 participants)

data_need.description: Larger, prospective, sex-specific studies on UPF consumption and infertility risk
data_need.why_it_matters: Without more and better-designed studies, it remains uncertain whether reducing UPF intake could lower infertility risk, particularly for women, who made up the vast majority of participants in existing data.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states evidence remains limited by few studies, substantial heterogeneity, and self-reported outcomes, and concludes 'Larger prospective, sex-specific studies are needed.'

dataset_source.note: The Human Reproduction periconceptional cohort study (also on PMC) is a prospective, couple-based study including both women's and men's UPF consumption in relation to fertility and early embryo development, addressing the sex-specificity gap; it is limited to couples undergoing infertility treatment/planning conception rather than a general population cohort, and male-specific prospective data overall remains far more limited than female data.

collection_guidance.note: The authors state that larger, prospective, sex-specific studies are needed to clarify the relationship between UPF consumption and infertility.

verification.findings: A new prospective study, "Periconceptional ultra-processed food consumption in women and men, fertility, and early embryonic development" (Human Reproduction, 2025), directly addresses this gap by examining UPF intake in both members of couples (not just women) in relation to fertility and embryonic development outcomes. A subsequent 2025/2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of UPF and infertility risk in adults found only four studies (8,769 participants total) and noted that only one prospective cohort estimate exists for male infertility, showing evidence is still sparse but growing and increasingly sex-specific.

paper.title: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment in women with polycystic ovary syndrome-a systematic review and meta-analysis.
paper.abstract:
Objective

To assess the effect of treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1-RAs) on weight-related, metabolic, and reproductive outcomes and health economics in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis, Prospero CRD42024535096.

Methods

Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and Medline were searched on September 20, 2024 for studies including women with PCOS, comparing GLP1-RAs with no treatment, placebo, lifestyle intervention, combined oral contraceptives, antiandrogenic drugs, or metformin in randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

Results

A total of 9654 studies were identified, 365 read in full text and 11 RCTs were included. GLP1-RAs as an add-on showed a reduction in BMI compared to the control group, mean difference (95% CI), -1.38 (-2.39 to -0.38) kg/m2 (low certainty). For LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, no difference was noted between the groups (low certainty), whereas evidence was insufficient to draw conclusion regarding glucose, insulin, hirsutism, and menstrual regularity. No studies were identified assessing quality of life, mental health, or cost-effectiveness outcomes.

Conclusion

GLP-1-RAs are associated with modest short-term weight loss in women with PCOS and overweight or obesity. Evidence for benefits on metabolic, reproductive, or psychological outcomes remains uncertain due to low-quality data, and no studies have evaluated cost-effectiveness.

Trial registration

The protocol for the systematic review was registered prospectively in Prospero, CRD42024535096.

problem.title: Uncertainty about whether GLP-1 receptor agonists improve metabolic, reproductive, and psychological health in women with PCOS
problem.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found GLP-1 receptor agonists led to modest weight loss when added to other treatments in women with PCOS and overweight or obesity. However, evidence on metabolic markers like glucose and insulin, reproductive outcomes like hirsutism and menstrual regularity, and psychological outcomes was insufficient or missing entirely. No studies evaluated cost-effectiveness.
problem.affected_women: Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who have overweight or obesity

data_need.description: Data on the effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists on quality of life, mental health, cost-effectiveness, glucose, insulin, hirsutism, and menstrual regularity in women with PCOS
data_need.why_it_matters: Without this evidence, clinicians and patients cannot judge whether GLP-1 receptor agonists meaningfully improve the reproductive, psychological, and economic aspects of living with PCOS, beyond short-term weight loss.

gap_evidence.note: The abstract states 'evidence was insufficient to draw conclusion regarding glucose, insulin, hirsutism, and menstrual regularity' and adds 'No studies were identified assessing quality of life, mental health, or cost-effectiveness outcomes.'

dataset_source.note: Covers glucose/insulin (HOMA-IR) and menstrual cycle outcomes from GLP-1RA RCTs in PCOS women via meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (search through Sept 2024) and a companion 2025 narrative review; does NOT address quality of life, mental health, cost-effectiveness, or hirsutism outcomes.

verification.findings: Newer systematic reviews and meta-analyses (2024–2025) now report on glucose, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), and menstrual cycle regularity in PCOS patients treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists, with a 2025 EJE systematic review/meta-analysis of 11 RCTs and a 2025 Endocrine Connections narrative review both describing improved glucose homeostasis and menstrual cycles, plus reduced BMI and testosterone. However, none of these newer sources report quality of life, mental health, or cost-effectiveness outcomes, and hirsutism data still appear limited or absent, so the original gap for those specific outcomes remains largely unfilled.
